title: Project 2
text:
R Code
library(tidyverse)
library(taylor)

data(package = "taylor")
data("taylor_album_songs")


This data was taken from TidyTuesday’s 2023-10-17 project, and originally came from Genius and the Spotify API.
Continuing with my Data Visualization from Project 1, here, I will look at Taylor Swift song lyrics.
Taylor Swift gets a lot of hate for supposedly overusing “car” as a rhyme with “bar”. I am very skeptical of this criticism, and so I will analyze how frequently she actually does this.


R Code
car_bar_data <- taylor_album_songs |>
  mutate(car = str_detect(lyrics, "\\b[Cc]ars?\\b")) |>
  mutate(bar = str_detect(lyrics, "\\b[Bb]ars?\\b")) |>
  mutate(car_bar =  car & bar) |>
  mutate(car_or_bar =  car | bar)


First, we will determine how frequently Taylor Swift rhymes car with bar per album.


R Code
ggplot(car_bar_data, aes(x = fct_relevel(album_name, album_levels), fill = car_bar)) +
geom_bar() +
labs(
title = "How Many Songs Rhyme Car with Bar?",
x = "Album",
y = "Number of Songs Per Album",
fill = "Song Rhymes Car with Bar?"
)+ coord_flip() + theme_minimal()









R Code
group_by(car_bar_data, album_name) |> 
  summarize(Percent = 100*sum(car_bar)/n())


# A tibble: 16 × 2
   album_name                    Percent
   <chr>                           <dbl>
 1 1989                             0   
 2 1989 (Taylor's Version)          0   
 3 Fearless                         0   
 4 Fearless (Taylor's Version)      0   
 5 Lover                           11.1 
 6 Midnights                        3.85
 7 Red                              0   
 8 Red (Taylor's Version)           0   
 9 Speak Now                        0   
10 Speak Now (Taylor's Version)     0   
11 THE TORTURED POETS DEPARTMENT    3.23
12 Taylor Swift                     0   
13 The Life of a Showgirl           0   
14 evermore                         5.88
15 folklore                         5.88
16 reputation                       6.67


This graph and table suggest that in the vast majority of her songs, Taylor Swift actually does not rhyme car with bar. In fact, even in her album Lover, which has the most instances of songs where Taylor rhymes car with bar, only 11.1 percent of the songs contain a car-bar rhyme. This seems to be enough evidence to dispute the claim that Taylor Swift is constantly rhyming car with bar
However, one might still be interested in how frequently bar and car are used as lyrics if they are not being rhymed with each other. The following plots show the number of songs that mentioned either cars or bars in each album, and for each plot, it shows how manyof those songs used car or bar as a rhyme for the word we are examining.
This first plot ony considers songs where Taylor Swift mentions cars, and the bars are filled in to show how many of these songs use car as a rhyme for bar.


R Code
ggplot(filter(car_bar_data, car), aes(x = fct_relevel(album_name, album_levels), fill = car_bar)) +
geom_bar() +
labs(
title = "How Many Songs Mentioning Cars also Mention Bars?",
x = "Album",
y = "Number of Songs Mentioning Cars",
fill = "Song Mentions Bars?"
)+ coord_flip() + theme_minimal()









This plot suggests that Taylor frequently mentions cars without feeling the need to rhyme car with bar.
This second plot ony considers songs where Taylor Swift mentions bars, and the bars are filled in to show how many of these songs use bar as a rhyme for car.


R Code
ggplot(filter(car_bar_data, bar), aes(x = fct_relevel(album_name, album_levels), fill = car_bar)) +
geom_bar() +
labs(
title = "How Many Songs Mentioning Bars Mention Cars?",
x = "Album",
y = "Number of Songs Mentioning Bars",
fill = "Song Mentions Cars?"
)+ coord_flip() + theme_minimal()









This plot suggests that there are fewer instances where Taylor mentions bars without also rhyming it with cars than the number of instances where Taylor mentions cars without rhyming it with bars. We can summarize these results:


R Code
  summarize(car_bar_data, Perc_Car_Bar_Rhymes = 100*sum(car_bar)/n(), Perc_Bar_Rhymes_Per_Car_Mentions = 100*sum(car_bar)/sum(car), Perc_Car_Rhymes_Per_Bar_Mentions = 100*sum(car_bar)/sum(bar), rhymes = sum(car_bar))


# A tibble: 1 × 4
  Perc_Car_Bar_Rhymes Perc_Bar_Rhymes_Per_Car_Me…¹ Perc_Car_Rhymes_Per_…² rhymes
                <dbl>                        <dbl>                  <dbl>  <int>
1                2.11                         15.9                   36.8      7
# ℹ abbreviated names: ¹​Perc_Bar_Rhymes_Per_Car_Mentions,
#   ²​Perc_Car_Rhymes_Per_Bar_Mentions


This table clearly shows that very few Taylor Swift songs actually feature car-bar rhymes (only 2.11 percent!), or 7 songs in total. It also shows Taylor is less likely to use bar on it’s own. 15.9% of the there time cars are mentioned, they are mentioned as a rhyme with bar, but 36.8% of the time bars are mentioned are they mentioned as a rhyme with car.
However, I do not believe that repeatedly rhyming cars with bars is initself a problem. Critics usually complain that rhyming cars with bars is indicative of lazy songwriting. Thus, if rhyming cars with bars is truly a valid critique, we would expect songs that rhyme cars with bars to be less musically varied than Taylor’s songs that do not rhyme cars with bars. In the next plot, we will compare the spread of 5 different ratings for Taylor Swift songs that rhyme car with bar, and those that don’t.


R Code
longer_car_bar_data <- car_bar_data |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(danceability, loudness, acousticness, instrumentalness, valence),  names_to = "what_var" , values_to = "what_val")

longer_car_bar_data |>
ggplot(aes(x = what_var, y = what_val, color = car_bar)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Scores of Songs Rhyming Car with Bar Vs Without", 
  x = "Type of Score", y = "Score (0-1)", color = "Song Rhymes Car with Bar") + coord_flip() + theme_minimal()









It seems like even for songs where Taylor rhymes car with bar, the songs vary greatly in terms of their danceability, loudness, acousticness, instrumentalness, and valence. Thus, it seems like rhyimg cars with bars is not actually as big of an issue as people claim. Taylor Swift’s songs that rhyme car with bars are just as varied in terms of sound as those that do not rhyme cars with bars.
Now that we’ve disputed the claim that Taylor Swift’s car-bar rhyming is an issue, I am interested in the other words that Taylor Swift could have rhymed with car. This plot shows the other words that Taylor uses in her songs, and the frequency that they appear in her discography.


R Code
how_many_cars_and_bars_data <- taylor_album_songs |>
  mutate(how_many_car = str_count(lyrics, "\\b[Cc]ars?\\b")) |>
  mutate(how_many_bar = str_count(lyrics, "\\b[Bb]ars?\\b")) |>
  filter(how_many_car > 0 | how_many_bar > 0)

#I took code from https://stackoverflow.com/a/58309991
# Posted by Slouei
# Retrieved 2026-10-14, License - CC BY-SA 4.0
# To figure out how to make the legend

ggplot(how_many_cars_and_bars_data) +
  geom_point(aes(x = album_release, y = how_many_car, color = "Car"), position = position_jitter()) + geom_point(aes(x = album_release, y = how_many_bar, color = "Bar" ), position = position_jitter())  +
labs(
title = "How Many Times Did Songs Mentioning Cars and Bars Mention Cars and Bars?",
x = "Song Release Date",
y = "Number of Car or Bar Mentions in Song") + theme_minimal()









R Code
#I had to look up the "unlist()" to make the list of lists into a list with objects
# Source - https://www.r-bloggers.com/2023/08/the-unlist-function-in-r/
all_ars_bad <- as.character(taylor_album_songs$lyrics) |> str_extract_all("\\b\\w+(?<!e)ars?\\b")

all_ars <- all_ars_bad |> unlist()

# I also had to look up a function that would make the list into a data frame
#source - https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/r-language/how-to-convert-a-list-to-a-dataframe-in-r/

all_ars_data <- as.data.frame(list(raw_words = all_ars)) |>
  mutate(lowercase_ars = str_to_lower(raw_words)) |>
  mutate(all_singular_ars = ifelse(str_detect(lowercase_ars, "s\\b"),str_sub(lowercase_ars, 1, str_length(lowercase_ars)-1), lowercase_ars)) |>
  group_by(all_singular_ars)|>
  summarize(ar_counts = n())


ggplot(all_ars_data, aes(x = fct_reorder(all_singular_ars, ar_counts), y = ar_counts)) +
geom_col(fill = "#2aaaa2") +
labs(
title = "Number of Times Words Rhyming with Car are Mentioned",
x = "Lyric",
y = "Number of Mentions"
) + coord_flip() + theme_minimal()









Combinatorialists rejoice! Taylor Swift is clearly a fan of stars and bars.
This plot suggests that out of all words that rhyme with “car,” Taylor Swift does indeed use the word “car” the most frequently. However, she clearly discusses many different car-rhymes.
I am also curious in how many times Taylor Swift sings words that contain “car” without mentioning car. This plot shows all the words in Taylor Swift lyrics that contain car, and their frequency in her discography.


R Code
all_car_bad <- as.character(taylor_album_songs$lyrics) |> str_extract_all("\\b\\w*[Cc]ar\\w*\\b")

all_car <- all_car_bad |> unlist()

all_car_data <- as.data.frame(list(raw_car_words = all_car)) |>
  mutate(lowercase_car = str_to_lower(raw_car_words)) |>
  mutate(all_singular_car = ifelse(str_detect(lowercase_car, "s\\b"),str_sub(lowercase_car, 1, str_length(lowercase_car)-1), lowercase_car)) |>
  group_by(all_singular_car)|>
  summarize(car_counts = n())


ggplot(all_car_data, aes(x = fct_reorder(all_singular_car, car_counts), y = car_counts)) +
geom_col(fill = "#2aaaa2") +
labs(
title = "Number of Times Words Contining Car are Mentioned",
x = "Lyric",
y = "Number of Mentions"
) + coord_flip() + theme_minimal()









Similar to the previous graph, while this graph does suggest that Taylor really likes the word “car,” she has many different lyrics that contain car, and so she may create rhymes based off of these, as well. For example, in the song “cardigan,” she rhymes “cardigan” with “car again.”

title: Golem Grad Tortoises
text:
R Code
library(tidyverse)

clutch_size_cleaned <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-03-03/clutch_size_cleaned.csv')
tortoise_body_condition_cleaned <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-03-03/tortoise_body_condition_cleaned.csv')


This data was taken from TidyTuesday’s 2026-03-03 project, which was curated by Novica Nakov, Free Software Macedonia. The data was originally collected by Dragan Arsovski, Xavier Bonnet, Ana Golubović, and Ljiljana Tomović, who presented it in their paper: Sex Ratio Bias Triggers Demographic Suicide in a Dense Tortoise Population.
Background
Over the generations, people have worked hard to build a society that grants men and women the same respect and opportunities, to varying levels of success. This issue transcends species, as the female tortoises in Lake Prespa in North Macedonia struggle with similar societal concerns. Unable to make their communities recognize them for their own autonomy, a female tortoise is often reduced to just “Hermann’s.”
Beyond their unfortunate name, the life of female Hermann’s tortoises on Golem Grad Island is incredibly heartbreaking. To paraphrase from the article and introduction on TidyTuesday: On an especially population-dense island in North Macedonia’s Lake Prespa, male Hermann’s tortoises vastly outnumber female Hermann’s tortoises. The sexually coercive males injure the female tortoises, and put them at risk of fatal falls. These harassed females are emaciated, tend to produce smaller clutches, and have lower annual survival rates than neighbouring mainland populations.
Data about the tortoises were taken from two locations on Golem Grad Island: the beach and the plateau. Data was also collected on the nearby mainland population of Hermann’s tortoises in Konjsko as a control.
Masses of Tortoises
The following plot shows the spread of masses of female vs male tortoises in the three different locations. From this plot, it is clear that the female tortoises in Konjsko tend to be heavier than those on the beach and on the plateau of Golem Grad, though the males at the three locations are comparable in size.


R Code
ggplot(tortoise_body_condition_cleaned, aes(x = sex, y = body_mass_grams, color = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() + facet_wrap(vars(locality)) + theme_minimal() +labs(title = "Mass of Females vs Males At Different Localities", x = "Sex and Locality", y = "Body Mass (grams)") + theme(legend.position = "none") 









Body Conditions of Tortoises
This plot shows the spread of the body condition index of the female and male tortoises in the three different locations. Body condition index refers to a tortoise’s mass scaled by its size. As stated by the original article, “Among the genus Testudo, the body condition of females is higher than that of males (Bonnet et al. 2010)”. However, from this plot, this is only true for the control group in Konjsko. The female tortoises in Golem Grad have similar BCIs to the males.


R Code
ggplot(tortoise_body_condition_cleaned, aes(x = sex, y = body_condition_index, color = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() + facet_wrap(vars(locality)) + theme_minimal() +labs(title = "Body Condition of Females vs Males At Different Localities", x = "Sex and Locality", y = "Body Condition Index") + theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Taylor Swift Songs
text:
R Code
library(tidyverse)

taylor_album_songs <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2023/2023-10-17/taylor_album_songs.csv')
taylor_all_songs <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2023/2023-10-17/taylor_all_songs.csv')
taylor_albums <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2023/2023-10-17/taylor_albums.csv')


This data was taken from TidyTuesday’s 2023-10-17 project, and originally came from Genius and the Spotify API.
Background
This dataset spans 17 years of Taylor Swift’s music career, from when she first released her debut album in 2006 to the week that the Eras Tour film premiered in October 2023. Thus, this dataset excludes the albums released afterwards, like the Taylor’s Versions of Speak Now and 1989, as well as the new albums, The Tortured Poets Department + The Anthology, and The Life of a Showgirl + The Encore (though this might be for the best, depending on who you talk to).
Danceability
Following the release of the “Shake It Off” music video in 2014, and again during The Eras Tour, Taylor Swift recieved mass amounts of online hate surrounding her dancing ability. Thus, it makes sense to track her songs’ danceability.
This boxplot shows the spread of Spotify Danceability Scores (1 being the most danceable and 0 being the least) for each of Taylor Swift’s albums. The plot is ordered in chronological order with her first album at the top. This spread suggests that Lover has the greatest spread in terms of how danceable the songs on an album are, and that her pop albums (1989, reputation, Lover, and Midnights) tend to be more danceable than her country albums (Taylor Swift, Fearless, and Speak Now).


R Code
ggplot(taylor_album_songs, aes(x = fct_rev(fct_relevel(album_name, "Taylor Swift", "Fearless (Taylor's Version)", "Speak Now", "Red (Taylor's Version)", "1989", "reputation" , "Lover" , "folklore" , "evermore", "Midnights")), y = danceability, color = album_name)) +
  geom_boxplot() + theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Taylor Swift" = "#52d1ab", "Fearless (Taylor's Version)" = "#b39e2d", "Speak Now" = "#935dd9", "Red (Taylor's Version)" = "#7d282b", "1989" = "#73b4c9", "reputation" = "#1a241c" , "Lover" = "#e3a6dd", "folklore" = "#b6bfbf", "evermore" = "#4d3323", "Midnights" = "#1d276e")) +
 theme(legend.position = "none") +
 labs(title = "Danceability of Taylor Swift Songs", y = "Album", x = "Spotify Danceability Score (0-1)") + coord_flip()
